concepts.title: Anther and Microsporangium Wall Layers
concepts.definition: A stamen carries a slender filament topped by an anther that is typically two-lobed and four-sporangiate; every microsporangium is jacketed by epidermis, endothecium, middle layers and an innermost tapetum.
concepts.key_idea: The tapetum feeds the growing pollen, while the outer three jackets shield the sporangium and help it split open at maturity.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebo101.txt lines 116-157 (stamen, anther section and microsporangium structure)
question_patterns: draw and label the four wall layers seen in a cross section of a microsporangium
how many microsporangia does a typical angiosperm anther hold
why is an anther described as dithecous and tetrasporangiate
which anther wall layer nourishes the developing pollen grains

solution_steps.action: Name the two parts of a stamen
solution_steps.explain: A long thin stalk, the filament, bears a terminal usually bilobed anther attached at the thalamus or petal.
Each lobe carries two theca, making the anther dithecous, and the four-sided organ holds four microsporangia, two per lobe, that ripen into pollen sacs.

solution_steps.action: List the wall layers from outside in
solution_steps.explain: Epidermis, endothecium and middle layers form the protective outer jackets; the tapetum lines the inside with dense, often multinucleate cells.

solution_steps.action: Assign functions and locate the sporogenous tissue
solution_steps.explain: Outer layers guard and later split to shed pollen, the tapetum nourishes grains, and compact sporogenous cells fill the centre of a young sporangium.

concepts.title: Microsporogenesis and Pollen Yield
concepts.definition: Inside each microsporangium the sporogenous cells act as pollen mother cells whose meiotic divisions produce haploid microspores, first stuck together in four-cell tetrads and later released as separate pollen grains.
concepts.key_idea: One diploid pollen mother cell meiotically yields a tetrad of four haploid microspores, and every microspore matures into exactly one pollen grain.
question_patterns: calculate the pollen grains produced from a given number of pollen mother cells in an anther
how many haploid microspores arise when a set of PMCs undergoes meiosis
find the total pollen grain output from microspore mother cells of a sporangium
a pollen mother cell divides meiotically; how many microspores and tetrads result
determine the pollen yield of an anther from its sporogenous cell count
work out how many functional pollen grains come from twenty sporogenous cells

solution_steps.action: Multiply the pollen mother cell count by four
solution_steps.explain: Meiosis in each diploid PMC produces a tetrad of four haploid microspores.
As the anther matures and dries, tetrad members separate and each microspore develops into one pollen grain, so the grain count equals the microspore count.
The sporangium's pollen output is four times its number of pollen mother cells.

worked_examples.question: Using Microsporogenesis and Pollen Yield, compute the result for pmc_count = 3.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Multiply the pollen mother cell count by four: microspores = pmc_count * 4 = 12.0 Step 2: Convert microspores to mature grains: pollen_grains = microspores = 12.0 Step 3: Report the final yield: result = pollen_grains = 12.0 Final result: 12.0

worked_examples.question: Using Microsporogenesis and Pollen Yield, compute the result for pmc_count = 4.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Multiply the pollen mother cell count by four: microspores = pmc_count * 4 = 16.0 Step 2: Convert microspores to mature grains: pollen_grains = microspores = 16.0 Step 3: Report the final yield: result = pollen_grains = 16.0 Final result: 16.0

concepts.title: Pollen Wall, Shedding Stage and Viability
concepts.definition: A pollen grain wears a chemically tough sporopollenin exine broken by germ pores over a thin cellulose-pectin intine, and it leaves the anther either two-celled or three-celled, remaining viable from half an hour in cereals to months in some other families.
concepts.key_idea: Sporopollenin resists heat, acids, alkalis and every known enzyme, which is why pollen survives as fossils, while germ pores mark the spots where the pollen tube later emerges.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebo101.txt lines 179-247 (pollen grain structure, 2-celled/3-celled stages, viability and storage)
question_patterns: name the outer and inner layers of a pollen grain wall and state what each is made of
why can pollen grains persist as fossils for very long periods
distinguish pollen shed at the two celled stage from pollen shed at the three celled stage
what purpose do the germ pores of the exine serve
how does pollen viability in cereals compare with that in some rosaceous or leguminous plants
describe how a pollen bank stores grains for use in crop breeding

solution_steps.explain: The hard outer exine is sporopollenin with apertures called germ pores; the thin continuous intine beneath is cellulose and pectin.

solution_steps.action: State the internal cells at shedding
solution_steps.explain: A mature grain holds a large food-rich vegetative cell and a small spindle-shaped generative cell; in over sixty percent of angiosperms it sheds at this two-celled stage, while elsewhere the generative cell has already divided mitotically into two male gametes, giving a three-celled grain.

Viability depends on temperature and humidity: cereals like rice and wheat lose it within about thirty minutes, some members of other families keep it for months, and grains of many species can be cryo-stored near minus 196 degrees Celsius in pollen banks for breeding programmes.

concepts.title: Ovule (Megasporangium) Structure
concepts.definition: An ovule grows on the placenta through a stalk called the funicle, joins it at the hilum, and wraps a reserve-filled nucellus in one or two integuments that leave a micropylar opening, with the chalaza forming the base opposite the micropyle.
concepts.key_idea: A single embryo sac, the female gametophyte, sits embedded in the nucellus of a typical ovule.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebo101.txt lines 248-285 (pistil parts and megasporangium structure)
question_patterns: label funicle hilum integuments micropyle chalaza and nucellus on a diagram of a typical ovule
which opening of the ovule lets the pollen tube enter
what connects the body of an ovule to the placenta
distinguish the micropylar end from the chalazal end of a megasporangium
why is the nucellus called a nutritive tissue of the ovule
how many embryo sacs does one ordinary ovule enclose

solution_steps.explain: The funicle attaches the ovule to the placenta; the point where funicle and ovule body fuse is the hilum.

solution_steps.action: Point out the protective envelopes and gap
solution_steps.explain: One or two integuments encircle the nucellus and stop short at the tip, leaving a small pore, the micropyle, opposite the basal chalaza.
The nucellus stores abundant reserve food and cradles the embryo sac, which usually occurs as a single copy per ovule.

concepts.title: Megasporogenesis, Monosporic Development and Embryo Sac Organisation
concepts.definition: A large, densely cytoplasmic megaspore mother cell in the micropylar nucellus divides meiotically into four haploid megaspores; three degenerate and the lone survivor, through repeated free-nuclear mitoses and later wall formation, builds an eight-nucleate, seven-celled embryo sac.
concepts.key_idea: Monosporic development means a single functional megaspore constructs the whole female gametophyte, ending with egg apparatus, antipodals and a two-polar-nucleus central cell.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebo101.txt lines 286-347 (megasporogenesis and female gametophyte development)
question_patterns: trace the steps from megaspore mother cell to a mature embryo sac
what does monosporic development of the female gametophyte signify
why do three of the four megaspores formed in an ovule degenerate in most flowering plants
how many mitotic nuclear divisions take a functional megaspore to the eight nucleate stage
are the divisions during embryo sac formation free nuclear or accompanied by walls
state the ploidy of the nucellus the megaspore mother cell and the functional megaspore

solution_steps.explain: The megaspore mother cell, set in the micropylar region of the nucellus, undergoes meiosis to give a linear row of four haploid megaspores.
Three megaspores wither away; only the functional one, usually the chalazal, enlarges and becomes the founder of the female gametophyte.
Its nucleus divides mitotically twice to opposite poles and then once more, giving two, four and finally eight nuclei, all before any cell wall appears.

Walls then partition six nuclei into cells: an egg flanked by two synergids with filiform thickenings at the micropylar pole and three antipodals at the chalazal pole, while the large central cell keeps the two remaining polar nuclei.
Maturity brings eight nuclei packed into seven cells, the standard angiosperm embryo sac.

concepts.title: Kinds of Pollination: Autogamy, Geitonogamy and Xenogamy
concepts.definition: Pollen movement is classified by source: autogamy lands pollen on the stigma of the same flower, geitonogamy moves it to another flower of the same plant, and xenogamy carries it between different plants, only the last delivering genetically unlike pollen.
concepts.key_idea: Closed cleistogamous flowers force self-pollination and assure seed set, whereas xenogamy alone counts as true genetic cross-pollination.
question_patterns: differentiate autogamy geitonogamy and xenogamy on the basis of pollen source
why is geitonogamy functionally cross pollination yet genetically similar to selfing
which pollination type brings genetically different pollen grains onto a stigma
how do cleistogamous flowers manage seed set without any pollinator
what two requirements must a flower fulfil for complete autogamy
name plants that bear both chasmogamous and cleistogamous flowers

solution_steps.action: Sort the three kinds by pollen origin
solution_steps.explain: Same flower gives autogamy; another flower on the same plant gives geitonogamy; a different plant gives xenogamy.
It needs a pollinating agent like a cross, but the pollen shares the plant's genotype, so genetically it matches selfing.
In Viola, Oxalis and Commelina, exposed chasmogamous blooms coexist with never-opening cleistogamous ones whose anthers dehisce inside the bud, guaranteeing autogamy even without pollinators.
Ordinary open flowers achieve autogamy only when pollen release matches stigma receptivity and the two organs sit close together.

concepts.title: Agents of Pollination and Floral Adaptations
concepts.definition: Wind, water and animals carry pollen between flowers, and each agent stamps a signature set of floral traits: light non-sticky pollen with feathery stigmas for wind, mucilage-coated ribbon pollen for water, and colour, scent plus nectar rewards for animal visitors.
concepts.key_idea: Biotic agents, especially bees, dominate pollination, and flowers pay for the service with nectar, pollen or egg-laying sites.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebo101.txt lines 422-564 (agents of pollination, wind water and animal examples)
question_patterns: list the floral adaptations that suit wind pollination
why do many water pollinated species coat their pollen in mucilage
how do animal pollinated flowers reward the creatures that visit them
compare wind pollinated and insect pollinated flowers in colour scent and nectar production
name the chief biotic pollinating agents of flowering plants
explain how pollination happens in Vallisneria and in the seagrass Zostera

solution_steps.action: Split the agents into abiotic and biotic
solution_steps.explain: Wind and water form the abiotic pair where pollen meeting stigma is a chance event, so vast surplus pollen is produced; animals form the biotic majority.
Well-exposed stamens, light non-sticky grains, often one ovule per ovary, many flowers per inflorescence and large feathery stigmas suit grasses and the corn cob.

In Vallisneria male flowers or pollen drift on the surface to female flowers raised on long stalks; in seagrasses like Zostera ribbon-like pollen travels underwater, shielded from wetting by a mucilaginous cover; most aquatic plants actually emerge and use insects or wind.

Large, colourful, fragrant, nectar-rich blooms attract insects, birds and bats; sticky pollen rides the visitor's body, and special deals exist, like the Yucca moth laying eggs in the ovary while pollinating, though some insects merely rob pollen or nectar.

concepts.title: Outbreeding Devices and Self-Incompatibility
concepts.definition: Flowering plants curb inbreeding depression by desynchronising pollen release from stigma receptivity, placing anthers and stigma far apart, blocking self pollen genetically through self-incompatibility, or producing unisexual flowers on the same or separate plants.
concepts.key_idea: Monoecy such as castor or maize still allows geitonogamy, but dioecy like papaya shuts out both autogamy and geitonogamy.
question_patterns: mention the strategies flowering plants evolved to discourage self pollination
what is self incompatibility and how does it stop self pollen from functioning
why does repeated self pollination cause inbreeding depression
how does dioecy differ from monoecy in blocking self fertilisation
explain how non synchronous pollen release and stigma receptivity prevent autogamy
which outbreeding device eliminates geitonogamy along with autogamy

solution_steps.explain: Continued self-pollination piles up homozygosity and lowers vigour and fertility, the condition called inbreeding depression.

solution_steps.action: List the timing and position devices
solution_steps.explain: Pollen may shed before or long after the stigma turns receptive, or the anther and stigma may sit at different spots so same-flower contact fails.
Self-incompatibility is a genetic barrier that halts pollen germination or tube growth in the pistil when the pollen carries the self profile.
Unisexual flowers on one plant (monoecious, as in castor and maize) rule out autogamy but not geitonogamy; sexes on separate plants (dioecious, as in papaya) rule out both.

concepts.title: Pollen-Pistil Interaction and Artificial Hybridisation
concepts.definition: The pistil chemically interrogates every landed grain, fostering germination and tube growth of compatible pollen while rejecting wrong or self pollen, and breeders exploit this gatekeeping by emasculating flower buds and bagging them so only chosen pollen reaches the stigma.
concepts.key_idea: Emasculation followed by bagging, dusting with desired pollen and rebagging guarantees a controlled cross, and unisexual female parents need no emasculation at all.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebo101.txt lines 585-665 (pollen-pistil interaction and hybridisation techniques)
question_patterns: describe the sequence of events covered by the term pollen pistil interaction
how does the pistil tell compatible pollen from incompatible pollen
why must emasculation be done before the anthers dehisce in a crossing programme
what role does bagging play in artificial hybridisation
under what condition can a breeder skip emasculation entirely
trace the route of the pollen tube from the stigma to the synergid

solution_steps.explain: Chemicals on the pollen surface converse with pistil tissues, and the pistil either promotes the grain or blocks its germination and tube growth.
The grain germinates through a germ pore; the tube grows through stigma and style, the generative cell dividing into two male gametes en route if the grain shed at the two-celled stage.
Guided by the filiform apparatus of a synergid, the tube enters the ovule through the micropyle and discharges its gametes.

For bisexual female parents remove undehisced anthers (emasculation), cover the bud with a butter-paper bag, dust receptive stigmas with selected pollen and rebag; for unisexual female flowers just bag, pollinate and rebag.

concepts.title: Double Fertilisation: Syngamy and Triple Fusion
concepts.definition: After the pollen tube empties into a synergid, one sperm unites with the egg to make a diploid zygote while the other unites with the two polar nuclei of the central cell to make a triploid primary endosperm nucleus, two fusions occurring together in a single embryo sac.
concepts.key_idea: Double fertilisation pairs syngamy with triple fusion and is exclusive to flowering plants, setting up embryo and endosperm side by side.
question_patterns: define double fertilisation and name its two component fusions
which nuclei participate in triple fusion and what does the fusion produce
why is the primary endosperm nucleus triploid
what becomes of the two male gametes released inside a synergid
explain why double fertilisation occurs only in angiosperms
state the ploidy levels of the zygote and the primary endosperm cell

solution_steps.explain: The tube releases both male gametes into the cytoplasm of one synergid of the embryo sac.
One gamete fuses with the egg cell nucleus, producing the diploid zygote that will grow into the embryo.
The second gamete joins the two polar nuclei in the central cell; three haploid nuclei merge into the triploid primary endosperm nucleus.
The central cell becomes the primary endosperm cell destined to form nutritive endosperm, and the paired events justify the name double fertilisation.

concepts.title: Endosperm, Embryo and Seed Development
concepts.definition: The primary endosperm cell multiplies ahead of the embryo, first as a free-nuclear tissue like coconut water and later cellular; the waiting zygote then passes through proembryo, globular and heart-shaped stages, and the finished ovule ripens into a seed inside a fruit whose wall derives from the ovary.
concepts.key_idea: Dicot embryos carry two cotyledons on an axis with epicotyl and hypocotyl, while grass embryos replace one cotyledon by a scutellum and sheathe their shoot and root tips in coleoptile and coleorrhiza.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebo101.txt lines 670-789 (endosperm, embryo, seed and fruit sections)
question_patterns: why does endosperm development start before embryo development
what is free nuclear endosperm and which familiar example shows it
differentiate albuminous and non albuminous seeds giving one example of each
describe the embryogeny stages of a dicotyledonous embryo in order
where do the scutellum coleoptile and coleorrhiza sit in a grass embryo
which maternal tissues give rise to the pericarp and the seed coat
what is perisperm and how does it differ from endosperm

solution_steps.explain: The PEN divides repeatedly without walls into a free-nuclear endosperm, later cellularising; tender coconut water shows the free-nuclear phase and the kernel the cellular phase, and embryos use this store for nutrition.
The zygote, held near the micropyle, divides only after some endosperm exists, then builds proembryo, globular, heart-shaped and mature stages of embryogeny.

A dicot embryo has two cotyledons, an epicotyl ending in the plumule and a hypocotyl ending in the radicle with root cap; a grass embryo has one scutellum, a shoot apex in a coleoptile and a radicle plus cap inside a coleorrhiza.

solution_steps.action: Finish with seed and fruit mapping
solution_steps.explain: Integuments harden into seed coats, the micropyle survives as a pore, the ovary wall becomes the pericarp, residual nucellus persists as perisperm in beet or black pepper, and seeds are albuminous (wheat, castor) or non-albuminous (pea, groundnut) depending on endosperm remnant.

concepts.title: Apomixis and Polyembryony
concepts.definition: Apomixis builds seeds with no fertilisation at all, either from an unreduced diploid egg or from nucellar cells, and when several embryos share one seed, as in Citrus and mango, the condition is polyembryony.
concepts.key_idea: Locking apomixis into hybrid crops would let farmers resow their own seed every season without the progeny losing hybrid character.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebo101.txt lines 851-909 (apomixis, polyembryony and hybrid seed significance)
question_patterns: what is apomixis and why does it matter to the hybrid seed industry
how does apomictic seed formation differ from ordinary sexual seed formation
define polyembryony and quote the plants where it is commonly seen
from which ovule tissue do the extra embryos of citrus seeds arise
why must hybrid seeds be produced afresh every year for the farmer
can apomictic embryos be regarded as clones of the mother plant

solution_steps.action: Define apomixis as asexual seed building
solution_steps.explain: Seen in some Asteraceae and grasses, it mimics sexual reproduction yet skips fertilisation, sometimes via a diploid egg formed without meiotic reduction.
More often, as in many Citrus and mango varieties, nucellar cells intrude into the embryo sac and grow into embryos, so one ovule carries many embryos.
More than one embryo inside a single seed is polyembryony, easy to spot by squeezing orange seeds.
Hybrid progeny normally segregate and lose yield, but an apomictic hybrid would breed true, sparing farmers the yearly cost of fresh hybrid seed.

worked_examples.question_pattern: A lobe of an anther contains {pmc_count} pollen mother cells that all complete meiosis. How many pollen grains will the resulting microspores finally give?

solution_template.explain: Each of the 25 PMCs forms a tetrad of 4 haploid microspores, so 25 * 4 = 100 microspores.

solution_template.action: Microspores become grains one to one
solution_template.explain: Tetrad members separate at anther maturity and each microspore matures into a single pollen grain.

worked_examples.question_pattern: A functional megaspore undergoes its nuclear divisions. Explain why the organ it produces is counted as eight-nucleate yet seven-celled at maturity.

solution_template.explain: Three successive mitotic cycles, all free-nuclear, lift the count from one nucleus to eight.
Walls enclose only six nuclei: egg plus two synergids at the micropylar end and three antipodals at the chalazal end.
The remaining two polar nuclei share one large central cell, so eight nuclei occupy seven cells.

worked_examples.question_pattern: Both male gametes of a pollen tube have just been discharged into a synergid. State what each gamete fuses with and give the ploidy of every product formed.

solution_template.explain: The first gamete meets the egg cell; their fusion (syngamy) yields a diploid zygote.
The second gamete joins the two polar nuclei; this triple fusion yields a triploid primary endosperm nucleus.
Because both fusions share one embryo sac, the phenomenon is double fertilisation, unique to flowering plants.

worked_examples.question_pattern: A plant species bears separate male and female flowers on every individual. Which kinds of selfing does this arrangement prevent, and which one could still occur if the sexes were on one plant?

solution_template.explain: Male and female flowers on different individuals is dioecy, as in papaya.
No same-flower transfer is possible (autogamy blocked) and no other flower of the same plant carries pollen for it (geitonogamy blocked).
With both flower sexes on one plant, as in castor or maize, autogamy still fails but geitonogamy between flowers of that plant can proceed.
